wine.name: Pegasus Bay Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, with a share of grapes touched by noble rot, botrytis, from parcels left on the vine to be picked late.
wine.sites: The estate's own vines at Waipara, many over thirty years old and a large share on their own roots, on free draining, north facing terraces in the lee of the Teviotdale hills, sheltered from the easterly sea breeze.
wine.making: When the vintage allows, some parcels are left to hang so that they come in with a share of noble rot. The free run juice is fermented slowly at cool temperatures to keep its fruit, and the wine is left off dry, its sweetness held by its acidity, in the house's long standing style.
wine.glass: Mandarin, green apple and kaffir lime with a honeyed hint of noble rot; taut and textural, its sweetness held in balance by fine acidity.
wine.ageing: Bright and fruity on release, it turns savoury and toasty with age and tastes drier as it does, and a good vintage lasts a decade or more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with spiced dishes or pork.

records.table: Off dry and long lived, Pegasus Bay Riesling is the family estate's own from the Waipara Valley, made with a share of nobly rotten grapes when the vintage allows and fermented slowly and cool. Mandarin, lime and a touch of honey; chill it lightly for spiced food.
records.story: The founder, a Christchurch neurologist, and his family began by making wine from grapes grown in their garden in the city, and by the house's account he planted one of Canterbury's early vineyards in 1976. In 1986 the family established Pegasus Bay in the Waipara Valley, an hour north of Christchurch, the four sons helping to take the cuttings and plant the vines, many of them on their own roots. The house tells that its Riesling block went in from 1987, and the first Pegasus Bay vintage was made in the family's garage in 1991, before the winery was built. What set the house apart was its embrace of noble rot. The long, dry autumns of the valley let Riesling ripen fully before botrytis sets in, and the family chose to keep a share of those grapes in its wines, building a range that runs from the dry Bel Canto through the off dry estate Riesling to the sweet Aria and Encore. The sons later took over the winemaking and the running of the estate. The estate Riesling is the key to that range, the bottle that proves a measure of noble rot can give off dry Riesling depth and a long life.

wine.name: Bell Hill Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the estate's own vines, the oldest of them on their own roots.
wine.sites: Small blocks on the slopes of a limestone hill in the Weka Pass, worked as a lime quarry until the late 1930s, planted from 1997 at very high density with the vines trained low to the ground.
wine.making: Aged for about twelve months in French oak barrels, much of them new in the house's habit, and in some years racked to tank for some months before bottling. The share of whole bunches changes with the vintage, and in some years the wine has gone to bottle without fining.
wine.glass: Cherry and violet over a chalky, savoury line; taut and fine grained, with bright acidity and fine tannin, and a silkier texture in riper years.
wine.ageing: Taut when young, it is built to keep, and reviewers give its strong vintages fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Bell Hill Pinot Noir comes from a tiny estate on an old lime quarry in the Weka Pass, planted from 1997 with the vines close together and low to the ground, as in Burgundy: cherry, violet and a chalky line. Pour it in a wide glass.
records.story: Limestone is rare in New Zealand, and the small hill near Waikari that gives Bell Hill its name was quarried for agricultural lime until the late 1930s. In 1997 two winemakers, who had worked a harvest together in Burgundy, came to the hill drawn by its limestone derived soils, and set out to grow only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay there. From 1997 to 2009 they planted the hill a small block at a time, at very high density, the ungrafted vines trained low to the ground in the Burgundian way. The first releases, from 1999 to 2002, were sold under the name Old Weka Pass Road; the first wine to carry the Bell Hill name came from the 2003 vintage, in a tiny quantity. The vineyard was certified organic by BioGro from March 2015. Bell Hill's wines were soon sought by collectors at home and abroad, and they gave North Canterbury's inland limestone a name of its own beside the Waipara Valley. Its Pinot Noir teaches what limestone gives New Zealand Pinot Noir: perfume, a chalky line and fine acidity rather than weight.

wine.name: Angel Flower Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from one block of the Waikari estate.
wine.sites: Angel Flower, a small, steep, north facing block of the Waikari estate on clay over limestone, planted from 2000 at very high density and farmed biodynamically from the start; it is the cooler and more exposed of the estate's two Pinot Noir blocks.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with the vineyard's own yeasts; in some years the fruit has been partly crushed by foot, and the share of whole bunches has changed with the vintages. The wine is raised mainly in older French oak barrels, with little new oak, before bottling.
wine.glass: Rose petal, dried herbs and summer berries over a savoury, chalky line; fine boned and cool in feel, with fresh acidity and fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Perfumed and open when young, it gains depth over some years in bottle, and older vintages have been released again from the estate's cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: On Pyramid Valley's biodynamic Waikari estate, Angel Flower Pinot Noir is the steep, north facing block of clay over limestone, planted in 2000 and named for yarrow. It smells of rose petal and dried herbs, and a young bottle opens with an hour in a decanter.
records.story: In 2000 a winemaking couple, inspired by the wines of Burgundy, chose a properly cool site of limestone, clay and marl in Pyramid Valley near Waikari and planted it, laying out the blocks by small changes in the soil and farming them biodynamically from the start. Each block was named for a meadow plant that grows in it, and each was bottled on its own. The first vintage from the estate came in 2006, from four foundation blocks: two of Pinot Noir, Angel Flower and Earth Smoke, and two of Chardonnay, Lion's Tooth and Field of Fire. In August 2017 the founders agreed to sell the estate to a new company formed to buy fine wine estates in New Zealand, whose first purchases were Pyramid Valley and Lowburn Ferry in Central Otago; the sale waited on the approval of the government's Overseas Investment Office. The new owners added a vineyard at Lowburn in Central Otago, consented in 2018, whose wines are bottled apart from the Waikari blocks. Angel Flower is a study in a single block: the same estate and the same hands as Earth Smoke, but a different slope and a different wine.

wine.name: Thomas Brothers Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from a single hillside block of the estate.
wine.sites: The Brothers Block, a steep, low yielding hillside block on the estate's highest slopes in the Omihi hills, on limestone soils that the house credits with a chalky tannin; certified organic.
wine.making: Hand picked and fermented with indigenous yeasts, then aged in French oak barriques, a large share of them new, for some fifteen to sixteen months, and bottled without fining or filtration. The house made it at first only in the years it judged strong enough.
wine.glass: Redcurrant, raspberry, plum and dark cherry with a savoury edge and the chalky tannin of its limestone; generous and rich in texture, yet fresh and long.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it holds and deepens for around a decade, the drinking window the house gives its 2023.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: From one steep block of limestone high in the Omihi hills comes Thomas Brothers Pinot Noir, Greystone's reserve from the Waipara Valley, with red and dark cherry fruit and a chalky grip. Under the name The Brothers' Reserve, its 2012 won a Decanter trophy.
records.story: Greystone takes its name from the limestone conglomerate that lies as bedrock under its vines. In 2000 the Thomas family found the land, an old sheep farm in the Omihi hills on the eastern side of the Waipara Valley, and by 2004, by the house's account, thirteen blocks of vines had been planted across its slopes of limestone and clay. The reserve Pinot Noir was made from special parcels of the estate only in the years the house judged worthy, and under the name The Brothers' Reserve its 2012 vintage won the International Trophy for Pinot Noir over fifteen pounds at the Decanter World Wine Awards of 2014, putting the young estate on the map abroad. From 2012 the house also began fermenting part of its Pinot Noir in open vessels set in the rows where the grapes grew, so that only the vineyard's own yeasts would take part, and it first released a Vineyard Ferment Pinot Noir of its own with the 2016 vintage. The estate turned to organic farming from 2014 and was certified by BioGro. In Thomas Brothers the house sets out what its highest limestone gives: a Waipara Pinot Noir of depth with a chalky line.

wine.name: Netherwood Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, a mass selection that the house believes descends from Mendoza clone cuttings.
wine.sites: The Netherwood vineyard, a south facing hillside planted in 1986 on Waipara Greensand, a green grey sandstone rich in glauconite; the old vines are dry farmed, on their own roots, and farmed organically and biodynamically.
wine.making: Made in very small amounts from the one hillside, a single barrel in 2019, it goes to bottle unfined and unfiltered, and the house holds it back so that it reaches the market with some bottle age.
wine.glass: Orange blossom, nectarine and white peach with hazelnut and almond; dense and textural through the middle, rich yet mouthwatering, with a fresh, salty line the house puts down to its sandstone.
wine.ageing: Released with some bottle age already, it has the density to keep for several years more, and the house advises opening it in a decanter.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant it, as the house advises; a wide white Burgundy glass.

records.table: A south facing hillside of Waipara greensand, planted in 1986, gives Black Estate its Netherwood Chardonnay, from dry farmed, biodynamic vines. Orange blossom, nectarine and hazelnut, dense and salty; it reaches the market with some bottle age, and the house would have you decant it.
records.story: Black Estate was begun at Omihi, on the eastern side of the Waipara Valley, by a restaurateur and his wife, who planted its Home vineyard in the early 1990s, in 1994 by the house's own account. Netherwood is older. The same founder had planted it in 1986 with a Waipara pioneer of Pinot Noir, on a south facing hillside of greensand, and the house calls it the first hillside planting in Waipara. In 2007 Black Estate was bought by a new family, a winemaking couple among them, who added the Damsteep vineyard at the foot of the Omihi Saddle, planted around the turn of the century, and for years bought fruit from Netherwood before buying the vineyard itself in 2015. The vineyards were certified organic by BioGro and, from 2022, biodynamic by Demeter, and each wine is labelled by the vineyard it comes from. Netherwood gives only a little Chardonnay, from old, dry farmed vines on their own roots, so the house holds it back to release with bottle age. Old vines and an unusual soil meet in it: a North Canterbury Chardonnay that tastes of its sandstone.
